content:
Quick answer: The best breakfast for arthritis is one that is easy to make on a stiff morning and follows NHS healthy eating advice: a wholegrain starchy food such as porridge or wholemeal toast, a protein food such as eggs, yoghurt, milk, beans or nut butter, and a portion of fruit. No breakfast cures arthritis, but this kind of meal supports energy, weight, bones and medicines that need food.

Evidence checked on 10 October 2026 against the NHS Eatwell Guide, NHS guidance on starchy foods, fibre and sugar, and NHS medicines information.

Mornings can be the hardest part of the day with arthritis. Stiff fingers make it difficult to open jars and cut bread, painful knees make standing at the kitchen counter tiring, and fatigue can mean you just want a cup of tea. It is easy to skip breakfast or grab a biscuit. Yet breakfast is a good chance to get fibre, protein and calcium, and some arthritis medicines need to be taken with food.

There is no magic "arthritis breakfast". No single food has been shown to treat arthritis. This guide gives practical, healthy breakfast ideas based on NHS advice, with options for good days and bad days.

What makes a good breakfast?

The NHS Eatwell Guide is a good template for any meal. For breakfast, aim for three things:

  1. A wholegrain starchy food for energy and fibre: porridge oats, wholegrain cereal, wholemeal or granary bread, or a wholemeal muffin. The NHS suggests choosing wholegrain cereals and says plain porridge with fruit makes a warming winter breakfast.
  2. A protein food to keep you full and support your muscles: milk, yoghurt, eggs, baked beans, nut butter, cheese, or fortified soya alternatives.
  3. Fruit or vegetables towards your 5 A Day: berries, banana, apple, tomatoes, mushrooms or spinach.

Breakfast is also a good time to have something that contains calcium, such as milk, yoghurt or a calcium-fortified plant drink, to help protect your bones.

Why breakfast matters with arthritis

  • Medicines. Some arthritis medicines should be taken with or after food. The NHS says naproxen, for example, should ideally be taken with or after food to help protect your stomach. Having a regular breakfast makes this easier.
  • Energy. A breakfast with fibre and protein gives steadier energy than a sugary one, which may help with fatigue.
  • Weight. A filling breakfast can make you less likely to snack on high-sugar foods later in the morning, which helps with weight management.
  • Fibre. The NHS says most adults eat about 20g of fibre a day and should aim for 30g. Breakfast is one of the easiest places to add fibre.
  • Protein spread. Many people eat very little protein at breakfast. Adding some helps spread protein across the day; see our protein guide.

Breakfast ideas

Porridge and oats

  • Classic porridge made with milk or fortified soya drink, topped with frozen berries (they thaw in the hot porridge) and a spoonful of ground flaxseed or chopped walnuts.
  • Microwave porridge pots or sachets: choose plain, unsweetened ones and add your own fruit. Flavoured varieties can be high in sugar.
  • Overnight oats: mix oats with milk or yoghurt in a jar the night before, and add grated apple or banana in the morning. No cooking needed, and a wide-necked jar with an easy lid helps if your hands are stiff.
  • Bircher-style muesli: unsweetened muesli soaked in milk with grated apple.

Eggs

  • Scrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with grilled tomatoes or wilted spinach.
  • Boiled eggs with wholemeal soldiers. Boil several at once and keep them in the fridge for quick breakfasts.
  • A vegetable omelette with peppers, mushrooms and spring onions (ready-chopped frozen vegetables work well).
  • Microwave scrambled eggs in a mug, if standing at the hob is hard.

Toast and bread-based

  • Wholemeal toast with peanut butter and sliced banana.
  • Baked beans on toast. Choose reduced-sugar and reduced-salt beans.
  • Sardines or mackerel on toast, a quick way to get oily fish, which the NHS recommends at least once a week.
  • Mashed avocado on toast with a squeeze of lemon and chilli flakes.
  • A wholemeal muffin with cottage cheese and tomatoes.

Yoghurt and cereal

  • Plain or Greek-style yoghurt with fruit and a sprinkle of oats or nuts. Flavoured yoghurts often contain added sugar, so plain with your own fruit is usually a better choice.
  • Wholegrain cereal such as shredded wholewheat, bran flakes or wheat biscuits with milk and sliced fruit.

Savoury and cultural options

A healthy breakfast does not have to look like a traditional British one. Many breakfasts from around the world fit the Eatwell Guide, for example vegetable upma or poha, ful medames with wholemeal bread, a Mediterranean plate of wholegrain bread, tomatoes, cucumber, olives, feta and an egg, or miso soup with tofu and rice. The key ideas are the same: wholegrains, protein, vegetables or fruit, and not too much salt, sugar or saturated fat.

Low-effort options for stiff, painful mornings

If your hands and joints are at their worst in the morning, plan ahead so breakfast takes almost no effort:

OptionPrep the night beforeMorning effort
Overnight oatsMix oats and milk or yoghurt in a jarAdd fruit and eat
Yoghurt pot with fruitNone (buy multipacks of plain yoghurt and pre-washed fruit)Open and eat
Boiled eggsBoil a batch and refrigeratePeel or eat from a cup
Microwave porridgeMeasure oats into a bowlAdd milk, microwave, stir
Wholemeal toast and nut butterNoneUse a toaster and a soft-spread nut butter
Banana and a glass of milkNoneMinimal

Practical tips:

  • Use a kettle tipper or a small, lightweight kettle filled with only what you need.
  • Choose easy-open packaging, or decant cereal and oats into containers with easy lids.
  • Pre-sliced bread and bananas are easier than loaves that need cutting.
  • Sit to prepare food if standing is tiring; a perching stool can help.
  • An occupational therapist can suggest kitchen gadgets that reduce strain on your hands.

What to limit at breakfast

  • Sugary cereals and granola. Many contain a lot of added sugar. The NHS says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day.
  • Fruit juice and smoothies. These count as free sugars. The NHS suggests limiting them to a combined total of 150ml a day. Whole fruit is a better choice. If you like smoothies, see our smoothie recipes and keep portions small.
  • Pastries, croissants and cereal bars, which are often high in saturated fat and sugar.
  • Processed meats such as bacon and sausages. Keep a full cooked breakfast as an occasional treat, or grill and add plenty of tomatoes, mushrooms and beans.
  • Too much butter or sugar on toast and porridge. Try unsaturated spreads, and sweeten porridge with fruit.

Some people find certain foods seem to affect their symptoms. Our guide to foods that may trigger symptoms explains how to test this without cutting out whole food groups.

Breakfast and your medicines

  • Take with food: some medicines, including NSAIDs such as naproxen and ibuprofen, are best taken with or after food to protect your stomach. Check your medicine leaflet.
  • Take before breakfast: some bone medicines must be taken on an empty stomach. The NHS says alendronic acid is usually best taken 30 minutes before breakfast, with plain tap water only, while sitting or standing upright, and you should stay upright for 30 minutes afterwards. Do not take it with tea, coffee, juice, milk or mineral water.
  • Grapefruit: grapefruit and its juice can interact with some medicines, including ciclosporin, colchicine and warfarin, according to Arthritis UK. Check with your pharmacist before having grapefruit at breakfast.
  • Warfarin: keep your intake of foods high in vitamin K, such as spinach, fairly steady rather than suddenly adding lots to breakfast.
  • Methotrexate days: if methotrexate makes you feel sick, dry toast, crackers or small regular meals may help. Tell your rheumatology team if nausea is a problem.

Drinks at breakfast

The NHS suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day, and says water, lower-fat milk, lower-sugar or sugar-free drinks, tea and coffee all count. A glass of water with your morning tablets and a cup of tea or coffee is a good start. Some people with arthritis drink less because getting to the toilet is difficult, but being dehydrated can make tiredness and constipation worse. If you take sugar in tea or coffee, try gradually reducing it. A milky drink such as a latte made with semi-skimmed milk or a fortified plant drink also adds calcium and some protein.

Breakfast on a budget

Healthy breakfasts can be some of the cheapest meals of the day:

  • A large bag of porridge oats makes many servings for a low cost per bowl.
  • Frozen berries are usually cheaper than fresh, keep for months and need no preparation.
  • Supermarket own-brand wholegrain cereals, plain yoghurt in large tubs and eggs are good value.
  • Bananas and apples are among the cheapest fruits.
  • Tinned sardines and baked beans are inexpensive sources of protein.

Buying the basics and adding your own toppings is usually cheaper and lower in sugar than flavoured pots, sachets and cereal bars.

If you have diabetes, gout or coeliac disease

  • Diabetes: wholegrain, higher-fibre options such as porridge and wholemeal toast with protein are usually better than sugary cereals. Your diabetes team or a dietitian can help with portions.
  • Gout: dairy foods, eggs, oats and fruit are generally suitable breakfast choices. Ask your GP or a dietitian about specific foods.
  • Coeliac disease: choose oats labelled gluten-free and gluten-free bread and cereals, and get advice from a dietitian.

A week of breakfasts

DayBreakfast
MondayPorridge with frozen berries and ground flaxseed
TuesdayScrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with tomatoes
WednesdayOvernight oats with grated apple and cinnamon
ThursdayPlain yoghurt with banana, oats and walnuts
FridayWholemeal toast with peanut butter and sliced banana
SaturdaySardines on toast with spinach, or a vegetable omelette
SundayGrilled cooked breakfast: poached egg, beans, grilled tomatoes and mushrooms, wholemeal toast

For lunches and evening meals to match, see our meal plans for arthritis.

Is there an anti-inflammatory breakfast?

Breakfasts based on oats, fruit, nuts, seeds, yoghurt, eggs and oily fish fit well with a Mediterranean-style diet, which NICE suggests for people with rheumatoid arthritis who want to change their diet. But NICE also says there is no strong evidence that diet changes will benefit arthritis itself. The benefit comes from your overall pattern of eating over time, not one meal. See our anti-inflammatory diet guide.

When to see a dietitian

Ask your GP or rheumatology team about a referral to a registered dietitian if you regularly skip meals because of pain or fatigue, have lost weight without trying, have diabetes and want help planning breakfasts, or follow a restricted diet. An occupational therapist can also help with kitchen equipment and ways to make food preparation easier.

When to get medical help

See your GP if you have indigestion, stomach pain or black stools while taking NSAIDs, or if nausea from your medicines stops you eating. See your GP if you are losing weight without trying or struggling to eat. Get same-day advice from your GP or NHS 111 if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with a fever.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best breakfast for arthritis?

One that is easy for you to make and includes a wholegrain starchy food, a protein food and some fruit, such as porridge with milk and berries or eggs on wholemeal toast.

Is porridge good for arthritis?

Porridge is a healthy, high-fibre breakfast that the NHS suggests, especially with fruit. It will not treat arthritis, but it fits well with an anti-inflammatory, Mediterranean-style diet.

Should I avoid eggs if I have arthritis?

No. Eggs are a good source of protein and contain some vitamin D. There is no good evidence that they make arthritis worse for most people.

Is it bad to skip breakfast?

Not necessarily, but it can make it harder to take medicines that need food and to get enough fibre, protein and calcium. If mornings are hard, try a low-effort option prepared the night before.

Are smoothies a good breakfast?

They can be part of one, but the NHS suggests limiting juice and smoothies to 150ml a day combined because they count as free sugars. Whole fruit with yoghurt is often a better choice.

Can I take my tablets with breakfast?

It depends on the medicine. NSAIDs are usually best with food, while some bone medicines such as alendronic acid must be taken before breakfast on an empty stomach. Check the leaflet or ask your pharmacist.
